algorithms.name: Sideslip-angle observer + adaptive/predictive path tracking (INRAE / Lenain et al.)
algorithms.reference: R. Lenain, M. Deremetz, J.-B. Braconnier, B. Thuilot, V. Rousseau, 'Robust sideslip angles observer for accurate off-road path tracking control', Advanced Robotics 31(9):453-467, 2017. Lineage: Lenain, Thuilot, Cariou, Martinet, 'Sideslip angles observer for vehicle guidance in sliding conditions: application to agricultural path tracking tasks', ICRA 2006 (RTK-GPS-only observer, farm tractor); 'Adaptive and predictive path tracking control for off-road mobile robots', European Journal of Control 13(4):419-439, 2007; 'Mixed kinematic and dynamic sideslip angle observer for accurate control of fast off-road mobile robots', J. Field Robotics 27(2):181-196, 2010 (seen only as a citation, content unverified). Advanced Robotics quartile unverified (probably Q2/Q3). The JFR and EJC papers are the Q1 anchors but predate 2018.
algorithms.core_idea: Extend the kinematic bicycle model with front and rear sideslip angles (beta_F, beta_R), modelled as slowly varying states. Estimate them online from RTK-GPS (plus heading) with an observer that does not depend on the reference path or speed. Then use exact feedback linearization (chained form) to command steering so that the lateral error converges despite sliding. The predictive term (MPC-style) anticipates the steering actuator lag and curvature changes.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Add ctrl='lenain_sso' to core.simulate. (1) Observer: run a steady-state Kalman/Luenberger observer, vectorized over (R,K), on the augmented state z=[d, psi, beta]. The model is d+=v sin(psi+beta)dt, psi+=v tan(delta)/l dt, beta+=w_beta (random walk, q_beta tuned). The measurements are meas (RTK-corrupted d) and psim. Linearize around d=psi=beta=0 for straight passes; the gain L comes from a discrete Riccati solve, like _lqr_gains. (2) Control: the chained-form law delta=atan(l/cos(beta_R)*( ... )); on straight lines this reduces to delta = atan( l*(-Kd*d_hat - Kp*sin(psi_hat+beta_hat))/(v*cos(psi_hat+beta_hat)) ) - beta_F_hat. With our single-beta model, set beta_F=beta_R=beta_hat. (3) Predictive actuator compensation: command delta_cmd(t)=delta_des(t+tau) using a 1-step-ahead prediction over tau=0.25 s, a first-order lag inversion clipped by rate_max. Use only meas, psim and the observer (never k_s, ou or rtk). Tune Kd, Kp, q_beta on the training fields with the same budget as the LQR-I baseline. Run it with every margin rule (nominal, fixed 5/10/30 cm, scenario, CVaR, worst-case, CE-U, CE-A). Report P(no miss), missed area, overlap, path length and passes, plus RMS lateral error and steering-rate RMS. Expected: the slope-driven component of e_k shrinks but the RTK component remains, so CE-U's q*sigma and overlap drop while the control-only + fixed-overlap rows still fail the 0.9 target.

algorithms.name: Receding-horizon estimation and control (MHE of traction parameters + NMPC), with DEM slope preview
algorithms.reference: E. Kayacan, S.N. Young, J.M. Peschel, G. Chowdhary, 'High-precision control of tracked field robots in the presence of unknown traction coefficients', Journal of Field Robotics 35(7):1050-1062, 2018, DOI 10.1002/rob.21794 (arXiv 2103.11294). Related: E. Kayacan, E. Kayacan, H. Ramon, W. Saeys, 'Learning in centralized nonlinear model predictive control: application to an autonomous tractor-trailer system', IEEE TCST 23(1), 2015, DOI 10.1109/TCST.2014.2321514 (MHE + NMPC; reported 6.44 cm mean error on a straight line). Slope-preview variant: a Chinese-language Nongye Jixie Xuebao (Trans. CSAM) paper puts a slope disturbance in the linear-MPC prediction model with adaptive weights (authors and year unverified).
algorithms.open_source_code: none from the authors; implement with acados (https://github.com/acados/acados), which supports MHE and NMPC, or CasADi
algorithms.core_idea: Unknown traction (slip) coefficients enter the kinematic model as parameters bounded in [0,1]. Moving-horizon estimation fits these parameters and the states over a sliding window of measurements. The NMPC uses the updated model, so steering accuracy holds as soil conditions change. The slope-MPC variant adds the predicted lateral slope disturbance to the prediction model, so the correction happens before the error appears.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Add ctrl='rhec_mpc'. (1) MHE: our slip is beta = -k_s*0.35*g_v + OU, which is linear in the unknown run-level k_s. Use a windowed least squares (window ~5 s) on measured lateral rates: d_meas_dot - v sin(psim) ≈ v*(-0.35 g_v_meas)*k_s + noise, with k_s constrained to [0,1.5]. This is the closed-form linear-in-parameter MHE. g_v_meas comes from the DEM at the measured position (the DEM is static map data that the planner also uses). Optionally add an IMU roll measurement roll_m = atan(g_v)+N(0,0.15 deg). (2) MPC: on a straight line the linearized error dynamics are LTI, so use an LQ preview controller (Tomizuka). Precompute the feedback gain and preview gains K_ff[j], j=0..N-1 (N≈60 steps = 3 s), offline from the Riccati recursion of the [d, psi, delta] model with steering lag tau. At run time delta_cmd = -K_fb x_hat - sum_j K_ff[j]*beta_pred[j], with beta_pred[j] = -k_s_hat*0.35*g_v(DEM at the look-ahead along-track point s+v j dt), then clip to delta_max and rate_max. This is exact unconstrained MPC and fully vectorized. As a fidelity check, run true constrained NMPC (acados) on a 20-field x 50-run subset and show it matches the preview LQ. (3) Feed it into every margin rule, as in item 1. This is the strongest 'fix it in control' competitor because it uses the same DEM that CE-A uses. If it still needs CE to certify coverage, the complementarity claim is established. For fairness against a well-specified model, also run a model-mismatch condition (nonlinear slip saturation, within-run k_s steps to mimic soil patches).

algorithms.name: Robust tube-based (N)MPC, used as controller + planner co-design (tube radius as swath margin)
algorithms.reference: E. Kayacan, E. Kayacan, H. Ramon, W. Saeys, 'Robust tube-based decentralized nonlinear model predictive control of an autonomous tractor-trailer system', IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics 20(1), 2015 (arXiv 2104.02063; NMHE for slip/side-slip + tube NMPC, bumpy grass field). Recent agricultural variant: 'Data-driven tube model predictive control of autonomous agricultural tractors for cross-slope navigation', ScienceDirect pii S2772375525000772 (journal likely Smart Agricultural Technology from the ISSN prefix; year ~2025, authors and quartile unverified): an LSTM predicts slope over the horizon inside a tube MPC.
algorithms.open_source_code: none from the authors; generic tube-MPC/RPI-set tools: acados (https://github.com/acados/acados); polytope RPI computation can be written in numpy, or use pytope (PyPI)
algorithms.core_idea: A nominal MPC steers a disturbance-free model, and an ancillary feedback u = v + K(x - x_nom) keeps the true state inside a robust positively invariant (RPI) tube around the nominal trajectory, given a bounded disturbance set W. The tube cross-section is a deterministic bound on the lateral deviation.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: This is the natural deterministic counterpart of CE and should be a headline competitor. (1) Controller: ctrl='tube_mpc' = nominal preview LQ (item 2) + ancillary LQR feedback (reuse K_lqri). (2) Disturbance set W: from the training fields, collect the one-step residuals w_t = x_{t+1} - A x_t - B u_t of slip + RTK noise. Build three W variants: max over training (W_max), 99th percentile (W_99), and data-driven per-slope-bin W(g) as in the LSTM-tube paper, with a simple binned predictor instead of an LSTM. (3) Compute the minimal-RPI outer approximation F_s = (1-alpha)^-1 * sum_{i<s} A_K^i W (Rakovic et al. 2005) and project it on d to get r_tube (or r_tube(x) along the pass for W(g)). (4) Planner: run the same greedy boustrophedon with h_k = w/2 - r_tube (pair margin = r_k + r_{k+1}). Report the same 5 metrics. Expected outcome: W_max is very conservative (heavy-tailed RTK), giving overlap at worst-case-baseline level. W_99 has no guarantee at the run level and should under-cover, because a run-level sup over ~thousands of steps exceeds the per-step 99th percentile. This shows why distribution-free run-level calibration (CE) is needed even with a robust controller.

algorithms.name: Learning-based (experience-based) predictive control for repetitive paths: GP/BLR-augmented MPC
algorithms.reference: C.D. McKinnon, A.P. Schoellig, 'Learn fast, forget slow: safe predictive learning control for systems with unknown and changing dynamics performing repetitive tasks', IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2019 (arXiv 1810.06681; weighted Bayesian linear regression + tube MPC; 900 kg ground robot, >2.7 km). Lineage: C.J. Ostafew, A.P. Schoellig, T.D. Barfoot, LB-NMPC with GP disturbance model learned from previous traversals (ICRA 2014) and its robust-constrained extension in IJRR 2016 (exact IJRR title unverified; 900 kg skid-steer robot, >5 km, up to 2 m/s).
algorithms.open_source_code: No official code found. Generic GP-MPC: https://github.com/helgeanl/GP-MPC (Python/CasADi). GP-MPC + MHE example: https://github.com/yassinekebbati/GP_Learning-based_MPC_with_MHE (MATLAB). https://github.com/learnsyslab/safe-control-gym (learning-based control benchmark; whether it has a GP-MPC module is unverified).
algorithms.core_idea: A simple a-priori model is augmented with a learned disturbance model (GP or weighted BLR) trained on experience from previous traversals. Its predictive mean is used as feedforward inside MPC, and its predictive variance tightens the constraints or tube, so the controller is cautious early and aggressive once data accumulate. Fast and slow learning lets it adapt to changed conditions.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Add ctrl='lbmpc'. Boustrophedon passes in one run are repetitive under a constant run-level soil condition (k_s, comp). (1) Online, within each run: after every pass k, fit a weighted BLR (or a sparse GP, using the GPyTorch or scikit-learn GP from PyPI) with features phi = [1, g_v, g_v|g_v|, sgn(pass)] to the residuals r_t = d_meas_dot - v sin(psim) that the nominal model cannot explain. Use a forgetting factor for 'fast' learning and a prior learned offline from the training fields for 'slow' learning. (2) Pass k+1 uses the BLR mean as preview feedforward in the item-2 preview-LQ MPC, and the BLR variance as a tube for an optional cautious margin. (3) Train the prior only on training fields and evaluate on the same test fields and runs. Because the simulator's slip is linear in g_v, this learner is well-specified and may look optimistic. Add the model-mismatch condition (slip saturation, within-run soil steps, steering deadband) so it is a fair competitor. Use it with CE-U/CE-A and the other margin rules, and also try 'LBMPC variance as margin' (h = w/2 - z_{1-eps}*sigma_BLR) as a learning-based uncertainty margin competitor.

algorithms.name: ESO/ADRC sideslip compensation: ESO-improved Stanley with sliding-mode heading control (and the composite backstepping-ADRC-SMC tractor controller)
algorithms.reference: 'Path Tracking Controller and System Design for Agricultural Tractors Based on Improved Stanley and Sliding Mode Algorithms Considering Sideslip Compensation', Agronomy (MDPI) 15(10):2329, published 1 Oct 2025, DOI 10.3390/agronomy15102329 (Jiangsu Univ. & Yangzhou Univ.; author names unverified; Agronomy is not a top Q1 agri-engineering venue). Companion: 'A Novel Control Method for Unmanned Agricultural Tractors: Composite Back-stepping Sliding Mode Path Tracking', Information Technology and Control, 2023 (time-varying ESOs + ADRC + SMC; authors unverified; reported to beat improved pure pursuit).
algorithms.core_idea: Lump slip, slope force, model error and other disturbances into one 'total disturbance' state. An extended state observer (ESO) estimates it in real time, and the controller cancels it. In the Agronomy paper the ESO gives a real-time sideslip-angle estimate that enters a Stanley law, with preview curvature compensation and a sliding-mode heading loop.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Add ctrl='eso_stanley' and ctrl='ladrc'. (a) ESO-Stanley: 3rd-order linear ESO on the lateral channel d_dot = v sin(psi) + f, where f absorbs v*beta. States z1≈d, z2≈f, with observer gains from bandwidth parameterization (Gao 2003: poles at -omega_o, omega_o≈3-5x the closed-loop bandwidth). beta_hat = z2/v. Steering: delta = -(psim + beta_hat) - atan(k*meas/v), plus a sliding-mode heading term with surface s = (psim+beta_hat) and a saturated switching gain (boundary layer phi), clipped to delta_max and rate_max. (b) LADRC on the second-order lateral dynamics d_ddot ≈ (v^2/l) delta + f_total: ESO with z1, z2, z3 (z3 ≈ total disturbance), u = (kp(0 - z1) - kd z2 - z3)/b0, b0 = v^2/l, then delta = u with lag compensation. Tune omega_c, omega_o, k and phi on training fields under the same budget. Expected: it removes slow slope-driven bias like item 1, but amplifies RTK noise at high observer bandwidth (waterbed effect). That makes a good 'controller tuning vs margin' trade-off plot: sweep omega_o and show the CE-U margin and overlap as a U-shape.

algorithms.name: Sliding-mode path tracking with nonlinear disturbance observer / adaptive (RBF) / fixed-time super-twisting SMC
algorithms.reference: J. Taghia, X. Wang, S. Lam, J. Katupitiya, 'A sliding mode controller with a nonlinear disturbance observer for a farm vehicle operating in the presence of wheel slip', Autonomous Robots 41(1):71-88, 2017 (offset kinematic model with front/rear lateral and longitudinal slip, matched and unmatched uncertainty, field experiments). Agricultural follow-ups: J. Li, Z. Shang, R. Li, B. Cui, 'Adaptive sliding mode path tracking control of unmanned rice transplanter', Agriculture (MDPI) 12(8):1225, 2022 (RBF-NN tuning; mean |lateral error| 9.1 -> 3.2 cm vs classical SMC in paddy field). 'Adaptive path tracking control of unmanned agricultural machinery with fixed-time super-twisting sliding mode based on RLS-ELM', Frontiers in Plant Science, 2025 (PMC12491169; authors unverified; reported 24.5%/27.4% lateral-error reduction vs two baselines).
algorithms.category: robust/adaptive sliding-mode control with disturbance observer
algorithms.core_idea: Define a sliding surface on lateral and heading error. The equivalent control comes from the kinematic slip model. A nonlinear disturbance observer (NDOB), an RBF network or an RLS-ELM estimate the lumped slip disturbance and compensate it, which reduces chattering and the needed switching gain. Super-twisting or fixed-time variants give finite-time convergence with continuous control.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Add ctrl='smc_ndob' and ctrl='stsmc'. Surface s = d_dot_hat + lambda*d_hat, with d_dot_hat = v sin(psim + beta_hat) and d_hat filtered from meas. NDOB: beta_hat_dot = L*(d_meas_dot - v sin(psim + beta_hat)), implemented as the standard p(x) auxiliary-variable form to avoid differentiating meas. Control: delta = atan( l/(v^2 cos(.)) * (-lambda v sin(psim+beta_hat) - eta*sat(s/phi)) ) for SMC+NDOB. For super-twisting: u = -k1 |s|^{1/2} sgn(s) + u2, u2_dot = -k2 sgn(s). Adaptive-RBF variant: an online RBF with Gaussian centres over (s, g_v) updated by sigma-modification. Respect rate_max and tau (chattering is penalized naturally by the rate limit). Also report steering-rate RMS and the share of samples at the rate limit, so 'wins' that come only from chattering are visible. Paddy fields (the user's southern data) have high slip, so this family is the most commonly cited Chinese-agri baseline and reviewers from CEA will expect it.

algorithms.name: Slip-aware pure pursuit (EKF slip estimation + look-ahead point offset) and optimal-goal-point pure pursuit
algorithms.reference: 'Path tracking control method for tracked agricultural vehicles based on slip-aware look-ahead point offset', Frontiers in Plant Science, 2025/2026 (DOI 10.3389/fpls.2025.1754679; PMC12813024; authors unverified). An EKF fuses RTK-IMU pose and track speeds to estimate slip online, offsets the look-ahead target by the estimated slip, and tunes the offset gain with PSO. Field tests at 0.35/0.75 m/s reported max lateral deviation -78.1% and mean -50.6% vs fuzzy pure pursuit. Also L. Yang et al., 'An optimal goal point determination algorithm for automatic navigation of agricultural machinery: improving the tracking accuracy of the Pure Pursuit algorithm', Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 194:106760, 2022 (seen only as a citation; method details unverified).
algorithms.open_source_code: No official code. The base pure pursuit/Stanley/rear-wheel-feedback/LQR/MPC reference implementations in https://github.com/AtsushiSakai/PythonRobotics (folder contents unverified in this session) can be adapted.
algorithms.core_idea: Keep the simple, robust pure-pursuit geometry, but (i) estimate slip online with an EKF and shift the look-ahead goal point laterally to pre-compensate the drift, and (ii) choose the look-ahead distance or goal point optimally rather than as a constant.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Our current pure_pursuit (Ld=4 m) is the uncompensated version, so add ctrl='pp_slip'. EKF on [d, psi, beta] (as in item 1, or reuse that observer) gives beta_hat. Goal-point offset: target lateral position y_goal = -(k_off * Ld * tan(beta_hat)); alpha = atan2(y_goal - meas, Ld) - psim; delta = atan(2 l sin(alpha)/Ld). Tune k_off and Ld with PSO (pyswarms on PyPI) or grid on training fields, minimizing the 95th percentile of |e_{k+1}-e_k|. Optimal-goal-point variant: choose Ld per step from a small candidate set {2,3,4,6,8} m by minimizing a predicted lateral error over 2 s with a 1-step model rollout (cheap, vectorized). It is a fair and cheap competitor because commercial and Chinese autosteer often run PP-family laws. It also shows the interaction finding: with uncompensated PP, slope-dependence of sigma is large, so CE-A should beat CE-U. With slip-compensated controllers, CE-A's advantage vanishes. Report this honestly. It explains the current null CE-A result under LQR-I.

algorithms.name: Commercial-style terrain compensation (IMU roll / antenna-height correction) + implement sidehill drift compensation
algorithms.reference: Patents: US7844378B2 'Farm apparatus having implement sidehill drift compensation' and US8489290B1 'Farm sidehill compensation' (roll from inclinometer/IMU, h_ant*sin(roll) correction, implement downhill drift compensation; assignee unverified). Academic context: IJABE paper noting slope and roughness errors under RTK and citing John Deere iTC terrain compensation (title and authors unverified). Not peer-reviewed algorithms; they stand for what commercial autosteer actually does.
algorithms.core_idea: Measure roll with an IMU and project the GNSS antenna position to the ground point (subtract h_ant*sin(roll)). Optionally add a slope-dependent feed-forward offset so the implement, which drifts downhill, is held on line.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Our simulator already contains partial roll compensation (cond.comp ~ 0.85 +/- 0.05). Add ctrl='tc_full' variants that represent vendor TC: (i) comp -> 1 with IMU roll noise N(0, 0.1-0.2 deg) and IMU bias N(0, 0.1 deg) per run, so meas = d + h_ant*(sin(roll) - sin(roll_m)) + rtk. (ii) Sidehill drift feed-forward: add a steady lateral reference offset y_ff = -c_s * g_v (c_s fitted on training fields by regression of steady-state d on g_v) on top of LQR-I. Combine with vendor-recommended overlaps (e.g., 5-10 cm, or a percentage of width) as the 'industry practice' row. This baseline answers the obvious reviewer question 'commercial autosteer already compensates terrain; why certify?' Expected: removes the roll part, not the RTK part, so P(no miss) with fixed overlap stays far from 0.9 while CE remains valid at lower overlap.

algorithms.name: Pass-relative (as-driven) guidance: next pass referenced to the recorded previous pass (AutoPath / contour-guidance style co-design)
algorithms.reference: Patents and industry systems: US11914379 'Methods and apparatus to generate a path plan' (guidance generator builds the next pass from leading/follower paths and their edges); US8583326 'GNSS contour guidance path selection'; John Deere AutoPath, row/boundary modes described by dealers (no peer-reviewed algorithm found; all fields unverified beyond titles and snippets).
algorithms.core_idea: Instead of fixed pre-planned parallel lines, generate pass k+1's reference online from the as-driven (recorded) trajectory of pass k, shifted by the working width minus a nominal overlap. Errors of pass k are then not compounded into a gap.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: This is the most direct 'adaptive re-planning' competitor to an offline certified margin. Implement in a new sequential simulate_relative(): simulate pass k, store the recorded measured offsets m_k(x) = d_k(x) + h_ant*... + rtk_k(t(x)), and set pass k+1's reference to y_{k+1}(x) = y_k + m_k(x) + (w - lambda) (smoothed with a 10 m moving average, curvature-limited). The controller (LQR-I or item 2) tracks this curved reference; feed reference curvature forward. The true pass-to-pass gap then contains only (rtk_k(t_k) - rtk_{k+1}(t_{k+1})) + tracking residual, not the systematic offsets. Compare (a) relative guidance + fixed lambda (0/5/10 cm), (b) relative guidance + CE-calibrated lambda (re-calibrate S on the relative-guidance runs; split CP remains valid because the whole closed-loop pipeline is exchangeable across runs), and (c) fixed parallel lines + CE. Report all 5 metrics; path length increases slightly with curved passes and number of passes may change. Expected: relative guidance reduces systematic error. Without CE it still has no guarantee, because temporally decorrelated RTK error and acquisition residuals remain. With CE it needs a smaller margin. This turns 'categories' into a real algorithmic co-design comparison.

algorithms.name: Implement offset-point predictive tracking (closed-form predictive control of the tool point)
algorithms.reference: S. Ngnepiepaye Wembe, V. Rousseau, J. Laconte, R. Lenain, 'A predictive control strategy to offset-point tracking for agricultural mobile robots', arXiv 2603.28439, Mar 2026 (preprint, not peer-reviewed; real field tests with two implements; median tracking error -24% to -56% and peak errors at curvature transitions up to -70% vs geometric, backstepping and model-based predictive baselines). Earlier: same authors, 'A novel control strategy for offset points tracking in the context of agricultural robotics', arXiv 2503.05835, 2025.
algorithms.open_source_code: none found (alphaXiv page suggests implementations on request; unverified)
algorithms.core_idea: Coverage is decided by where the implement (an offset point rigidly attached behind or beside the vehicle) actually goes, not by the rear-axle point. The controller predicts the evolution of the offset-point lateral error over a finite horizon and minimizes it with a closed-form (solver-free) predictive law. It also shows that exact tracking of a reference by a rigidly attached tool is generally impossible.
algorithms.how_to_adapt_to_our_problem: Our evaluation uses the lateral offset of the vehicle reference point. Add an implement point at longitudinal offset L_imp (e.g., -1.5 to -3 m behind the rear axle), with lateral position d_imp = d + L_imp*sin(psi + beta), and evaluate coverage on d_imp (implement footprint of width w centred there). Add ctrl='offset_mpc': predict d_imp over horizon H (2-3 s) with the linearized model and choose delta in closed form to minimize sum (d_imp_pred)^2 + r*delta^2. With constant delta over H this is a scalar quadratic in delta, so it is closed-form and vectorized. Compare with LQR-I tracking the rear axle. Under slope with crab angle beta, rear-axle tracking leaves an implement offset L_imp*sin(beta) that this controller removes. Then apply CE-U/CE-A on d_imp. This also improves the realism of the paper (coverage = implement footprint) and adds a 2026 state-of-the-art controller from the leading agricultural-robotics control group.

notes:
HOW TO USE THESE CONTROLLERS TO ANSWER THE USER'S Q1 CRITIQUE (compare algorithms, not only categories; figures collapse to one point):

1) Positioning argument for the paper, which also supports the theory. Any controller that uses GNSS feedback tracks the MEASURED position. The true lateral error is e = S(z)*w_slip - T(z)*n_rtk, and the complementary sensitivity T is about 1 inside the closed-loop bandwidth. So slow RTK drift and multipath (our real i2Nav series) passes straight to the ground, whatever the controller. Slip-compensating controllers (items 1-7) shrink the S*w part; raising observer or controller bandwidth amplifies RTK noise (waterbed effect). 'Fix it in control' therefore lowers sigma but cannot certify P(no missed area) >= 1-eps. CE complements every controller, and the paper should show that with named published algorithms.

2) Experimental matrix ('algorithms x margin rules'):
- Controllers: PP, Stanley, LQR, LQR-I (existing), plus Lenain SSO, RHEC/preview-MPC, tube-MPC, LB-MPC (BLR/GP), ESO-Stanley/LADRC, SMC-NDOB/STSMC, slip-aware PP, vendor TC, pass-relative guidance, offset-point MPC.
- Margin rules: nominal, vendor fixed overlap, the existing statistical baselines (scenario, CVaR, DRO, worst-case, CQR), tube radius (item 3), LB-MPC variance margin (item 4), and CE-U/CE-A/CE-pair.
- Same fields, runs, RTK segments and seeds (common random numbers, which gives paired Wilcoxon tests). Same tuning budget for every controller (e.g., 100 Optuna trials on training fields; objective = 95th percentile of |e_{k+1}-e_k|).
- Metrics: the user's 5 metrics, plus RMS lateral error, steering-rate RMS and percentage of time at the rate limit (exposes chattering 'wins'), and compute time per step.
- Fairness: the controller may only see meas, psim, an IMU roll measurement with noise, odometry speed and the static DEM. It must never see k_s, ou, comp or rtk.
- Because our slip model is linear in side slope with a run-constant k_s, model-based and learning controllers are well-specified. Add a model-mismatch condition (slip saturation, within-run soil-patch steps in k_s, steering deadband/backlash) so the comparison is not biased toward them, and also not toward CE.

3) Figures that do not collapse:
(a) For each controller, sweep the margin lambda from 0 to 40 cm and plot the continuous P(no miss) vs overlap% curve (a risk-coverage frontier), with the CE operating point and each baseline's point marked. Controllers separate horizontally (better control means less overlap at equal risk) and baselines spread along the curves.
(b) Missed area per run (cm^2/ha, log scale, violin or ECDF). This is informative even where P(no miss)=0, so methods at P=0 no longer pile onto a single dot.
(c) Heatmap of controller x margin rule, showing P and overlap, with cells that fail certification hatched.
(d) Bar chart of overlap saved relative to LQR-I+CE, by controller.
(e) Controller-bandwidth sweep (ESO omega_o or LQR weights) vs CE margin, which shows a U-shape (waterbed).
(f) Interaction plot: CE-A minus CE-U gain under PP/Stanley (uncompensated, strongly slope-dependent sigma) vs under slip-compensated controllers. This should turn the current null CE-A result into an explained finding.

4) Other items seen in search, lower priority or out of the date window:
- ILC for farm-vehicle trajectory tracking (Acta Automatica Sinica 2014, D-type ILC; IEEE TVT 2025 analysis showing ILC on Stanley/PP approaching NMPC). It could be a 'spatial ILC across passes' variant of item 4.
- Fnadi, Du, Plumet, Benamar, constrained MPC for a bi-steerable rover on slippery ground, Control Engineering Practice 107:104693, 2020/2021.
- Soitinaho & Oksanen, NMPC for agricultural tractor local navigation, IEEE TCST 31(5):2043-2054, 2023.
